newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. drug chief to start heroin unit in Colombia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drug chief to start heroin unit in Colombia.

text.p: U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration head Thomas Constantine began a lightning visit to Colombia on Tuesday during which he was expected to sign an accord to set up a bi-national heroin-fighting unit.

The DEA director will spend only six hours in the country and hold talks with National Police chief Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano and Col. Leonel Gallego, head of the police anti-drug unit, embassy officials said.
He was to place a plaque at Colombian police headquarters commemorating those agents that died in the war on drugs.

Constantine will not meet with President Ernesto Samper, whom U.S. officials say is a "truly corrupt president" in the light of allegations that he accepted $6 million in drug money to finance his 1994 presidential campaign.

The DEA estimates Colombia supplies more than 80 percent of the world's cocaine and said that South American heroin, primarily from Colombia, accounted for 62 percent of all heroin seized in the United States in 1995 -- more than from southeast Asia's Golden Triangle.
In a recent Reuter interview Gallego said Colombia could be producing as much as five tonnes of heroin a year.

He said exports of heroin from Colombia were virtually unknown before 1991, adding that since the breakup of the Medellin and Cali drug cartels "a new breed of drug lord" had emerged revolving around the production and trafficking of heroin.

In 1997 the United States awarded about $80 million in counternarcotics aid to Colombia and a multi-million-dollar package of material aid, which included cropdusters, helicopters and fast riverboats.
Last week the State Department freed about $70 million in additional aid to the Colombian military to be used in combating drugs. The Colombian army and police play a lead counternarcotics role.

The United States blacklisted, or decertified, Colombia for the second consecutive year in March for its failure to crack down hard enough on drug trafficking but the move does not affect aid used in the anti-drug fight.
